supplementary_news.content_title: How chronic illness can raise the risk of severe dengue
supplementary_news.content: Dengue can be more dangerous in people with chronic illnesses, while a second infection with a different virus type may also increase the risk of severe disease. (Pixabay pic) PETALING JAYA : Grace Ooi thought she knew what dengue felt like. She had first contracted the illness in secondary school and spent several days in hospital. But when dengue struck again in 2013, the experience was far more severe. Her fever rose and fell for almost a week, and by the time she was admitted, her platelet count had dropped to single digits. She needed a blood transfusion and spent three days in intensive care. “I didn’t know a second dengue infection could be more severe, or that having hypertension could make things worse,” said Grace, now 45 and living with diabetes and hypertension. Her experience highlights a risk many people may not realise: dengue can become more dangerous in those with chronic illnesses, while a second infection with a different virus type can also carry a greater risk of severe disease. According to communications minister Fahmi Fadzil, the number of dengue cases in the country rose by 66% to 65,979 as of epidemiological week 35 this year, compared with 39,616 cases recorded during the same period last year. The health ministry has linked the increase partly to dengue’s cyclical pattern and a shift in the dominant virus type, with DENV-3 now circulating widely. Consultant emergency physician Dr Ganasan Chelladurai said the patients he sees affected most are often older adults living with obesity and diabetes. “When they come to us late, management becomes much more difficult,” he said. His message is simple: do not wait for dengue to look serious before taking it seriously. Dengue may start with fever, body aches and lethargy. But in some people, the illness can worsen just as the fever subsides. Warning signs include persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, spontaneous bleeding, difficulty breathing, marked weakness, confusion, poor appetite or sudden deterioration. Ganasan recalled a young man who arrived at the emergency department with vomiting, diarrhoea and exhaustion but no fever. Only when questioned did he mention having had a fever three days earlier. Dr Ganasan Chelladurai. His blood pressure and platelet count were low, and testing confirmed dengue. Ganasan said this can be a crucial turning point, when complications such as bleeding or dangerously low blood pressure may develop rapidly. “The fever can disappear just as complications begin,” he said, adding that older people and those with chronic illness may deteriorate more quickly. When the body is already under strain Conditions including diabetes, hypertension, heart or kidney disease and obesity have been associated with a greater likelihood of severe dengue, although the level of risk varies. A 2026 study of hospitalised adults in northern Vietnam found that those with chronic conditions were about twice as likely to develop severe dengue. Another study in Brazil found a much higher death rate among hospitalised dengue patients with certain underlying illnesses. That does not mean everyone with a chronic condition will develop severe dengue, or that otherwise healthy people are safe from complications. But those with underlying conditions may need earlier assessment and closer monitoring. One case still weighs heavily on Ganasan. A man in his early 50s who had diabetes and obesity, and who smoked, continued working through two days of fever and body aches because he was his family’s sole breadwinner. By the fourth day, he could barely get out of bed, eat or drink. Yet he feared hospital admission would cost him his next job and the income his family depended on. He sought emergency care only after vomiting blood. Despite transfusions and intensive care, he died, leaving his wife to care for two young children without savings or a financial safety net. Ganasan remembers her asking: “Doctor, I don’t know how to take care of my children. I don’t know how to move on.” For him, the case is a reminder that dengue’s consequences can extend far beyond the patient. Fogging can help reduce adult mosquito populations in affected areas, but it works best alongside measures such as removing stagnant water where mosquitoes breed. So, why was Grace’s second experience with dengue worse than the first? A previous dengue infection usually provides long-lasting protection only against that particular virus type, not all four. A later infection with a different type can carry a greater risk of severe disease. DENV-3 is not automatically more infectious or dangerous than other dengue virus types. Its significance lies partly in population immunity: people who have not encountered it remain susceptible, while those previously infected with a different type may face a greater risk during a later infection. A shift in the dominant virus type may, therefore, leave more people vulnerable, while chronic illness remains a separate factor that can influence severity. For Ganasan, the priority is to look at the whole person: age, underlying conditions, previous dengue history and how quickly symptoms are changing. Ultimately, prevention still matters. Removing stagnant water, covering water containers, using repellents and screens, wearing protective clothing and joining neighbourhood clean-ups all remain important. Vaccination can add another layer of protection for some people, and those interested can speak to a healthcare professional about whether it is appropriate for them. “Dengue does not affect only the person who falls ill,” Ganasan stressed. “The cases I have seen show how it can disrupt an entire family – the people caring for the patient, the children who depend on them and the plans they have made together.” “That is why prevention matters. We each need to prevent breeding, protect ourselves from bites and act early when symptoms appear.”

supplementary_news.content_title: Florida reports spike in dengue fever cases, health alerts issued
supplementary_news.content: Florida is experiencing an increase in dengue fever cases originated in-state, with 33 cases in Tampa Bay alone and 41 statewide as of Sept. 1. According to Fox 13 Tampa Bay , the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) reported 30 cases in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County. The Florida Department of Health has placed Hillsborough and Pinellas counties under mosquito-borne illness alerts. Dengue is a viral disease caused by four related viruses, with fever being a common symptom, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention . The virus is most prevalent in subtropical and tropical areas of the world, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. While it is less common in the U.S., cases of the virus have appeared in Florida, Texas, Hawaii, California, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands. 2024 was a record year for dengue in the U.S., according to the CDC . Mosquito-control crews in Florida are increasing treatments and urging homeowners to cover or empty standing water, dress in long sleeves and closed-toed shoes outdoors and use repellent containing DEET or oil of lemon eucalyptus. supplementary_news.content: Metro Phoenix Sports Things To Do Politics Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals STATE Florida dengue cases jump again, with most cases found in 1 county Dengue is sometimes called breakbone fever because of the severe pain it causes Cheryl McCloud USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Sept. 11, 2026, 5:20 a.m. MT Dengue fever surges in Florida with 38 new cases in one week. Cases of dengue fever — sometimes called breakbone fever — have jumped again in Florida, with 38 new locally acquired cases reported in one week by the Florida Department of Health. That brings the statewide total of dengue cases to 111 for the year as of Sept. 5. ➤ Meet the mosquito, the world's deadliest animal Hillsborough County continues to lead the state in the number of locally acquired cases of dengue, jumping from 59 to 95 confirmed cases in one week. The FDOH is also seeing a few confirmed cases of West Nile virus, although none have been reported since Brevard County issued a mosquito-borne illness advisory Sept. 3. Currently, 11 counties are under either a mosquito-borne illness advisory or mosquito-borne illness alert. Shop Amazon for mosquito repellents The mosquito-borne illnesses are among several monitored by the state agency. Here's what you should know about mosquito-borne illnesses in Florida, symptoms to watch for, and how best to prevent mosquito bites. How many types of mosquito-borne illnesses are there in Florida? FDOH compiles weekly data on the following mosquito-borne viruses in a report called "Florida Arbovirus Surveillance": West Nile virus (WNV) Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV) St. Louis encephalitis virus (SLEV) Dengue virus (DENV) Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) Zika virus (ZIKV) California encephalitis group viruses (CEV) Malaria Mosquito-borne illness alerts, advisories issued for these Florida counties A mosquito-borne illness advisory has been issued for the following counties: Alachua Brevard Duval Leon Orange Palm Beach Pasco Walton A mosquito-borne illness alert has been issued for the following counties: Hillsborough Miami-Dade Pinellas "A mosquito-borne illness advisory means the public should take precautions to reduce mosquito bites due to factors indicating local disease such as positive sentinels, very few presumptive or positive human cases, or other justifications," according to Sarasota County. "A mosquito-borne illness alert means that there has been heightened disease activity, a significant increase in vector (disease capable) mosquito populations, or an increase in locally-transmitted human cases. "Residents should continue to take precautions, but exercise additional caution in preventing mosquito bites." Is dengue spreading in Florida? See counties reporting mosquito-borne illnesses According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Sept. 5, there have been 111 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported, which is up from 73 since Aug. 29. There also have been along with two cases of West Nile virus: Dengue: 111 cases 95 in Hillsborough County (which jumped from 59 the week before) 7 in Miami-Dade County 5 in Pinellas County 2 in Pasco County 1 in Orange County 1 in Palm Beach County West Nile: 2 1 in Alachua County 1 in Walton County What are symptoms of dengue, breakbone fever? "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: sudden onset of fever severe headache eye pain muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. "Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. The disease is often diagnosed incorrectly because the symptoms are similar to influenza and other viruses," the CDC said. "Around one out of every 20 people infected by a dengue virus develops severe dengue, a life-threatening medical emergency that requires immediate medical attention," according to YaleMedicine. Why is dengue called 'breakbone fever?' Dengue is sometimes called “breakbone fever” because, in addition to fever, "it can cause severe aches and pains, especially in the legs, joints, and back," according to YaleMedicine. Dengue does not actually cause bones to break, according to YaleMedicine. Is dengue contagious? Dengue is spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people through bites. The Centers for Disease Control said a woman who is infected with the dengue virus during pregnancy could pass the virus to her fetus, causing death to the fetus, low birth weight or premature birth. Can dengue be treated? "While there is no cure for dengue and there are no specific medications for the condition, getting adequate hydration and plenty of rest, and taking acetaminophen for pain and fever can help alleviate symptoms while the body’s immune system fights the virus," according to YaleMedicine. "In most cases, people recover from dengue within a week. For those with severe dengue, treatment by health care professionals can significantly lower the risk of death." What are symptoms of West Nile virus? "West Nile virus is a mosquito-borne flavivirus that causes mild to severe illness," the Florida Department of Health said. "Approximately 80% of people who are infected with WNV will not show any symptoms at all." Mild symptoms include: fever headache body aches nausea vomiting Sometimes swollen lymph glands or a skin rash on the chest, stomach and back. Symptoms can last from a few days to several weeks. About one in 150 people infected with West Nile will develop severe illness. Symptoms include: high fever headache neck stiffness stupor disorientation coma tremors convulsions muscle weakness vision loss numbness paralysis "These symptoms may last several weeks, and neurological effects may be permanent. Severe illness can also result in death," FDOH said. "People usually do not get sick enough to go to the hospital. For this reason, many people might not realize they have been infected." What are the best mosquito repellents to use? According to the Florida Department of Health, repellents with the following active ingredients provide the best protection: DEET Picaridin IR3535 Oil of lemon eucalyptus Para-menthane-diol 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient 'Drain and cover' helps keep mosquitoes away The FDOH offered this advice to help keep mosquitoes away from your Florida home: Drain Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Cover If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up. Apply mosquito repellent to exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. Sandip Nayak September 16, 2026 Supported by Delhi-NCR is seeing a rise in dengue cases as the monsoon continues, with Delhi recording 432 cases in 2026, including 121 in September up to September 12, according to the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD). The latest figures show September has recorded the highest monthly dengue count so far this year, with 71 new infections reported in the preceding week. West Delhi has reported the highest number of cases, followed by Central Delhi and Shahdara North. MCD has intensified mosquito-control measures, while health experts are urging residents to focus on preventing stagnant water and seeking medical attention for persistent fever or warning signs. Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh has also stressed that preventing seasonal diseases requires participation from communities, schools, resident welfare associations and local representatives, saying the aim is to provide the right information without creating panic. Cases Rise Due To Monsoon The latest MCD data shows 432 dengue cases in Delhi this year, compared with 619 during the corresponding period in 2025, 709 in 2024 and 2,097 in 2023. West Delhi has recorded 57 cases, followed by Central Delhi with 54 and Shahdara North with 50. Civic authorities have inspected more than 2.79 crore houses for mosquito breeding this year, finding active larvae in around 1.47 lakh homes. More than 1.10 lakh legal notices have also been issued over conditions that could support mosquito breeding. Dr Suranjit Chatterjee, Senior Consultant, Internal Medicine, Indraprastha Apollo Hospitals, said the increase is closely linked to conditions allowing Aedes mosquitoes to breed, adding that the issue is not simply rainfall but what happens afterwards. He stressed that resident welfare associations, schools and workplaces also have a role in prevention. Know The Symptoms And Warning Signs Dengue is transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes, which are primarily active during the daytime. Common symptoms include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and rash. However, severe dengue can develop after the fever begins to fall. The World Health Organization (WHO) lists severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, extreme tiredness, restlessness, unusual thirst and pale or cold skin as warning signs requiring immediate medical care. There is no specific antiviral treatment for dengue. WHO recommends medical assessment, adequate fluids and rest, with paracetamol used for fever and pain when appropriate. Aspirin and ibuprofen should be avoided because they can increase the risk of bleeding. The Logical Indian’s Perspective Dengue prevention cannot be treated as the responsibility of hospitals or civic authorities alone. As Delhi’s September numbers show, tackling mosquito-borne diseases requires sustained action at the household and community level. Emptying coolers, flowerpot trays, buckets and other containers that can collect water, keeping water-storage vessels covered, using mosquito repellents and seeking timely medical advice can all help reduce risk. At the same time, civic bodies must continue surveillance, sanitation and mosquito-control efforts, particularly in areas where breeding is detected. The goal should be awareness without unnecessary fear, and collective action without blaming individuals or communities. What more can residents, schools, housing societies and civic authorities do together to keep Delhi-NCR safer from dengue? supplementary_news.content_title: How To Spot Dengue Fever Symptoms Early
supplementary_news.content: Warm coastal weather makes outdoor living fantastic, but humid subtropical climates are also ideal breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Florida health officials recently raised concerns after confirming 10 locally acquired cases of dengue fever across two Gulf Coast counties, with 8 in Hillsborough County and 2 in Pinellas County. While Florida has logged nearly 150 total dengue cases statewide this year, the vast majority were contracted abroad by travelers who brought the virus home before local mosquitoes could pick it up. Even though the nationwide risk of widespread transmission remains low, local cases warrant prompt attention, given how the virus affects the body. Medical researcher Tunde Rasheed tells Blavity Health, "Dengue is a viral disease spread by infected female Aedes mosquitoes, and is commonly referred to as 'breakbone fever' because it causes painful muscle, joint and bone aches. It can cause intense physical pain and vascular problems that can prove life-threatening." These localized outbreaks extend beyond Florida, as states like Texas, Hawaii, Arizona and California have also seen small pockets of transmission. Shifting climate patterns and expanding insect habitats are gradually widening the geographic footprint of traditionally tropical diseases. Staying safe comes down to simple awareness: knowing the early warning signs, understanding how the virus behaves and taking proactive steps to avoid mosquito bites while enjoying the outdoors. What is dengue fever? Dengue fever is an acute viral illness caused by any of four closely related serotypes of dengue virus, known as DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4. These pathogens are in the Flaviviridae family, which includes yellow fever, West Nile virus and Zika virus. Dengue is the fastest-growing mosquito-borne viral disease in the world, according to data from the World Health Organization (WHO). Every year, nearly 400 million people are infected worldwide, with about 100 million having symptoms and thousands dying, mostly in tropical and subtropical climates. PubMed Central explains that female Aedes mosquitoes infected with the virus are the primary carriers of the disease; the most common species are Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus, the latter known as the Asian tiger mosquito. Aedes spp. are daytime biters, with the highest biting activity in the early morning and late afternoon before sunset; also, unlike many common nuisance mosquitoes. Although the majority of patients with dengue have been imported from people traveling to endemic areas of the Caribbean, Central America, South America and Southeast Asia, there are established populations of Aedes mosquitoes in the southern states of the U.S., so that a visiting traveler with the live virus could infect a local person with the virus by being bitten by a local mosquito. Which country has the most dengue fever? Brazil consistently has the highest number of dengue fever cases worldwide. Surveillance data released by the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) indicate that the Americas experience frequent cyclical dengue epidemics, and Brazil has reported a large number of suspected and confirmed cases each year. The country's wide tropical climate, urban population, monsoon-season rainfall and widespread distribution of Aedes aegypti create conditions for continuous transmission. Other countries with frequent reporting of a high burden of severe dengue include Paraguay, Argentina, Colombia, Peru and much of Southeast Asia, including Indonesia, Vietnam, the Philippines and Thailand. Climate change has expanded the range of vectors in recent years, bringing warmer winters and longer rainy seasons to previously unaffected temperate high-altitude areas in South America and Southern Europe. What's happening in your body An infected Aedes mosquito deposits the dengue virus directly into the dermis (the layer under the skin) when feeding on humans. The viral particles bind immediately to dendritic cells, the frontline immune cells located in the outermost layers of the skin, according to a study published by the National Institutes of Health (NIH). These immune cells are not neutralized but are "hijacked" by the pathogen. The virus invades cells and multiplies in the cytoplasm; infected cells are carried to regional lymph nodes, which disseminate the virus throughout the lymphatic system. Fresh viral particles are now available in the general circulation from the lymph nodes, and primary viremia occurs. The virus attacks circulating monocytes and macrophages and infects endothelial cells in microcapillaries. In response, the immune system releases large amounts of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, triggering a robust inflammatory cascade that affects the entire body. This "hyper-inflammatory state" alters blood vessel permeability, leading to tiny cracks between the cells lining them, allowing plasma to leak into the tissues. At the same time, the virus inhibits the bone marrow's ability to produce megakaryocytes, which are precursor cells that produce blood platelets. It also produces antiplatelet autoantibodies, which cause platelet counts to fall to very low levels (thrombocytopenia). Dirt walls in the capillaries, low platelet counts and ineffective clotting mechanisms contribute to plasma loss, significant drops in blood pressure and internal bleeding. Causes of dengue fever The basic reason for the occurrence of dengue fever is the presence of an infected person, a mosquito vector and a susceptible person. The uninfected mosquito must feed on a person in the viremic phase of the infection, which usually lasts from the last day of incubation through the first 4-5 days of acute fever. The virus enters the insect, infects midgut cells, and enters an extrinsic incubation period of 8-12 days. The virus circulates in the mosquito during this period until it reaches the glands that secrete saliva. After the salivary glands become infected, the mosquito can spread the virus for the duration of its life (2-4 weeks in nature). Environmental factors beyond biological transmissions greatly accelerate the spread of the virus. The Aedes female mosquito is a "container breeder" and can be found in artificial water containers. Unused car tires, dirty birdbaths, dirty roof gutters, flowerpot saucers, exposed rain barrels and plastic pet bowls with water in them make great nurseries. Their eggs can dry out and persist on container walls for months without water, and rain easily stimulates egg hatch, leading to sudden local outbreaks of mosquitoes. Mosquitoes that bite you are probably breeding in your own backyard, as Aedes mosquitoes are not known to stray more than 150 feet from their own hatching sites. Eliminate items that hold standing water, such as flowerpot saucers, pet water bowls, tarps and birdbaths, once a week. Cleaning the walls of containers will dislodge sticky mosquito eggs, which can last for months under dry conditions. Health risks and complications Most people with dengue recover within 1 to 2 weeks, but about 1 in 20 will develop severe dengue, formerly called dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF) or dengue shock syndrome (DSS). The Mayo Clinic defines severe dengue as a life-threatening medical emergency characterized by systemic vascular collapse. As capillary permeability increases, large amounts of fluid escape into the space around the lungs (pleural effusion) and the space in the abdomen (ascites). This sudden loss of the intravascular volume causes severe hypovolemic shock and profound hemodynamic instability with loss of oxygen delivery to vital organs. In addition, severe deficiency in platelets and platelet dysfunction lead to spontaneous bleeding. Patients may have persistent gum bleeding, nosebleeds that can't be controlled, bleeding of the gastrointestinal system (GI bleeding) that may lead to bloody vomit or black tarry stools, and large hematomas under the skin. PubMed Central notes that acute liver injury, heart failure and inflammation of the central nervous system, such as encephalitis, can also occur during severe dengue. Severe dengue deaths can be over 20% if not treated promptly and correctly in a hospital with intensive care facilities and having experts in managing intravenous fluids. Still, with early supportive hospital treatment, the death rate is below 1%. One of the most dangerous immunological interactions is known as antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), which is why reinfection is considered more dangerous. Once a person has had dengue, they are immune to that serotype for the rest of their life. They, however, acquire only partial, short-term cross-immunity against the other three serotypes. When that person is re-infected months or years later with a different serotype, the non-neutralizing antibodies produced by the previous infection bind to the new virus without destroying it. Still, they aid the virus in entering host macrophages and greatly stimulate viral replication, thereby increasing the likelihood that an individual will be severely affected by the infection and develop life-threatening disease. What to do about dengue fever symptoms As dengue is viral, there are no antiviral prescription medicines to cure the infection. Treatment is mainly symptomatic and involves careful fluid management and avoiding antithrombotic drugs. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is the only medication approved for over-the-counter sale for high fever and debilitating muscle aches. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin, naproxen and ibuprofen should be completely avoided by patients and caregivers. NSAID use during a dengue infection significantly increases the risk of major internal gastrointestinal bleeding due to NSAIDs' blood-thinning properties, impairing normal platelet aggregation and causing stomach irritation. Oral hydration is the key to outpatient recovery and must be done continuously and aggressively. To replace electrolytes lost due to excessive sweating, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, patients should drink balanced fluids, such as oral rehydration salts, broth and coconut water (not plain tap water alone). When to see a doctor If you suddenly develop a high fever with severe headaches, pain behind the eyes or intense joint aches, you should seek medical attention, especially if you live in an area with a local transmission alert or have recently traveled to tropical countries or regions. The most serious phase for any dengue patient is the critical phase, the period when the first high fever subsides and drops below 100°F (38°C), occurring 3-7 days after the onset of the disease. Vascular leakage can suddenly worsen during this transition period, which will take 24-48 hours. The Mayo Clinic says that immediate medical attention is crucial if you or a family member experiences signs of severe dengue. In addition to the relentless, severe abdominal pain or tenderness, other critical physical symptoms are persistent vomiting (fluids are not retained at least 3 times within 24 hours). Similarly, it's important to be aware of any signs of unusual bleeding, such as blood in the stool or vomit, blood on the gums, nose or mucous membranes. Other critical red flags include alterations in circulation, breathing and mental status. Get immediate assistance if the person has rapid, shallow breathing or is short of breath at rest. Sudden dizziness when standing, with cold, clammy, unusually pale skin, may be a sign of circulatory collapse. Also, when the systemic stress is severe, there may be dramatic changes in cognition and behavior, including very low energy, restlessness, confusion, disorientation or great difficulty waking. Special laboratory blood tests are ordered to confirm an active infection, such as reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) to detect viral RNA or enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) to detect the dengue nonstructural protein 1 (NS1) antigen in the first week of illness. Later in the course of the disease, IgM and IgG antibody panels are used to confirm the immune response. What does a dengue fever rash look like? A dengue rash has two phases: a pale, transient pink rash on the face and neck that appears within the first 48 hours of fever, and a second rash that develops after the fever has subsided. Three to six days later, a second rash appears, which is quite distinctive and appears as bright red, measles-like maculopapular spots all over the back, arms and legs, sometimes with small, round islands of perfectly normal pale skin in between, what dermatologists call "white islands in a sea of red." How do doctors treat severe dengue in the hospital? Severe dengue is managed in an inpatient or intensive care unit with meticulous intravenous fluid therapy, regular monitoring for plasma leakage as indicated by hematocrit levels and platelet transfusion for uncontrolled hemorrhage, and support of blood pressure and organ perfusion. "There's four different types of dengue and what has happened in the past when you get severe dengue infection is that you've been infected with one type of dengue virus," USF Health virologist and associate professor of medicine Dr. Michael Teng said. "And then you get infected with a different type of dengue virus, and your immune system doesn't protect you from that second type of the virus, but it makes things worse." Bottom line Dengue fever is a painful, mosquito-borne viral disease transmitted by daytime -biting Aedes mosquitoes that causes severe fevers, debilitating body aches, and retro-orbital headaches. Although clusters of local transmission, such as the one in Florida, have been relatively small, about one in 20 people with dengue can develop more serious complications that include life-threatening plasma leakage, internal bleeding, and vascular shock. Taking care to avoid mosquito bites outdoors, eliminating standing water around the house, using only acetaminophen to treat pain, and getting medical attention right away if the belly hurts or the nausea doesn't settle down are important. Frequently Asked Questions How long does dengue fever last? Acute symptoms of dengue fever typically last between two and seven days, with the vast majority of individuals recovering fully after about one to two weeks. However, mild fatigue and joint stiffness can linger for several weeks afterward. Is it safe to be around someone with dengue? Yes, it is entirely safe to be around an infected individual because dengue is not contagious and cannot spread directly from person to person through casual contact, respiratory droplets, saliva or touch. supplementary_news.content_title: Avoiding antibody-dependent enhancement enables dengue prevention and treatment
supplementary_news.content: Background: Dengue virus is one of the most widespread vector-borne viral pathogens in the world. Nearly 400 million dengue virus infections occur each year, resulting in approximately 20,000 deaths. In addition, dengue-associated illness comprises an annual global economic burden of around $9 billion USD. While dengue is rare in the continental U.S., warming patterns across the Southern U.S. are expanding the range of mosquito species capable of transmitting the virus. There is currently no FDA-approved dengue vaccine for use in individuals who have not experienced a previous dengue virus infection, or any approved monoclonal antibody therapy for the prevention or treatment of acute dengue. Technology overview: This Upstate Medical University technology overcomes a major challenge in dengue prevention and treatment: Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE). This phenomenon causes IgG isotype antibodies that recognize dengue virus to enhance infection in individuals with waning or incomplete antiviral immunity. Our technology circumvents this challenge by 1) providing immediate immunity to infection by providing dengue virus neutralizing antibodies , and 2) utilizing an IgA1 antibody construct that will preserve antibody function while being incapable of facilitating ADE like IgG antibodies. This not only provides immediate protection against dengue infection in individuals who have not had dengue before, but also reduces the risk of developing severe disease in individuals with preexisting/suboptimal dengue immunity. Advantages: Enables the development of dengue prevention and treatment options by avoiding Antibody Dependent Enhancement. Applications: There are several potential applications for this product: Travelers: reduce the risk of infection while in dengue-endemic areas. US Military: reduce the risk of infection and prevent the loss of combat effectiveness when deployed in dengue-endemic areas. Residents of dengue endemic areas during dengue transmission seasons Relatives, neighbors, or other living in close proximity to an individual experiencing an acute dengue infection. supplementary_news.content_title: How chronic illness can raise the risk of severe dengue
supplementary_news.content: Dengue can be more dangerous in people with chronic illnesses, while a second infection with a different virus type may also increase the risk of severe disease. (Pixabay pic) PETALING JAYA : Grace Ooi thought she knew what dengue felt like. She had first contracted the illness in secondary school and spent several days in hospital. But when dengue struck again in 2013, the experience was far more severe. Her fever rose and fell for almost a week, and by the time she was admitted, her platelet count had dropped to single digits. She needed a blood transfusion and spent three days in intensive care. “I didn’t know a second dengue infection could be more severe, or that having hypertension could make things worse,” said Grace, now 45 and living with diabetes and hypertension. Her experience highlights a risk many people may not realise: dengue can become more dangerous in those with chronic illnesses, while a second infection with a different virus type can also carry a greater risk of severe disease. According to communications minister Fahmi Fadzil, the number of dengue cases in the country rose by 66% to 65,979 as of epidemiological week 35 this year, compared with 39,616 cases recorded during the same period last year. The health ministry has linked the increase partly to dengue’s cyclical pattern and a shift in the dominant virus type, with DENV-3 now circulating widely. Consultant emergency physician Dr Ganasan Chelladurai said the patients he sees affected most are often older adults living with obesity and diabetes. “When they come to us late, management becomes much more difficult,” he said. His message is simple: do not wait for dengue to look serious before taking it seriously. Dengue may start with fever, body aches and lethargy. But in some people, the illness can worsen just as the fever subsides. Warning signs include persistent vomiting or diarrhoea, severe abdominal pain, spontaneous bleeding, difficulty breathing, marked weakness, confusion, poor appetite or sudden deterioration. Ganasan recalled a young man who arrived at the emergency department with vomiting, diarrhoea and exhaustion but no fever. Only when questioned did he mention having had a fever three days earlier. Dr Ganasan Chelladurai. His blood pressure and platelet count were low, and testing confirmed dengue. Ganasan said this can be a crucial turning point, when complications such as bleeding or dangerously low blood pressure may develop rapidly. “The fever can disappear just as complications begin,” he said, adding that older people and those with chronic illness may deteriorate more quickly. When the body is already under strain Conditions including diabetes, hypertension, heart or kidney disease and obesity have been associated with a greater likelihood of severe dengue, although the level of risk varies. A 2026 study of hospitalised adults in northern Vietnam found that those with chronic conditions were about twice as likely to develop severe dengue. Another study in Brazil found a much higher death rate among hospitalised dengue patients with certain underlying illnesses. That does not mean everyone with a chronic condition will develop severe dengue, or that otherwise healthy people are safe from complications. But those with underlying conditions may need earlier assessment and closer monitoring. One case still weighs heavily on Ganasan. A man in his early 50s who had diabetes and obesity, and who smoked, continued working through two days of fever and body aches because he was his family’s sole breadwinner. By the fourth day, he could barely get out of bed, eat or drink. Yet he feared hospital admission would cost him his next job and the income his family depended on. He sought emergency care only after vomiting blood. Despite transfusions and intensive care, he died, leaving his wife to care for two young children without savings or a financial safety net. Ganasan remembers her asking: “Doctor, I don’t know how to take care of my children. I don’t know how to move on.” For him, the case is a reminder that dengue’s consequences can extend far beyond the patient. Fogging can help reduce adult mosquito populations in affected areas, but it works best alongside measures such as removing stagnant water where mosquitoes breed. So, why was Grace’s second experience with dengue worse than the first? A previous dengue infection usually provides long-lasting protection only against that particular virus type, not all four. A later infection with a different type can carry a greater risk of severe disease. DENV-3 is not automatically more infectious or dangerous than other dengue virus types. Its significance lies partly in population immunity: people who have not encountered it remain susceptible, while those previously infected with a different type may face a greater risk during a later infection. A shift in the dominant virus type may, therefore, leave more people vulnerable, while chronic illness remains a separate factor that can influence severity. For Ganasan, the priority is to look at the whole person: age, underlying conditions, previous dengue history and how quickly symptoms are changing. Ultimately, prevention still matters. Removing stagnant water, covering water containers, using repellents and screens, wearing protective clothing and joining neighbourhood clean-ups all remain important. Vaccination can add another layer of protection for some people, and those interested can speak to a healthcare professional about whether it is appropriate for them. “Dengue does not affect only the person who falls ill,” Ganasan stressed. “The cases I have seen show how it can disrupt an entire family – the people caring for the patient, the children who depend on them and the plans they have made together.” “That is why prevention matters. We each need to prevent breeding, protect ourselves from bites and act early when symptoms appear.”

supplementary_news.content: Chennai Tamil Nadu India World Entertainment Entertainment Cinema OTT G.D.N Business Sports Lifestyle Technology Videos Explainers Editor's Picks Chennai Fever cases rise in Chennai, dengue surveillance intensified The figures assume significance as the city enters a period of intermittent rainfall, which can create conditions favourable for mosquito breeding Dengue DT NEXT Bureau Updated on: 16 Sep 2026, 2:21 am Copied Follow Us CHENNAI: Chennai has reported a rise in fever cases in recent weeks, with 140 dengue infections detected among more than 2,000 fever cases reported during the first 10 days of September, prompting health authorities to intensify surveillance and vector-control measures across the city. The figures assume significance as the city enters a period of intermittent rainfall, which can create conditions favourable for mosquito breeding. In August, around 4,500 fever cases were reported, including 160 dengue infections. Adyar, Anna Nagar and Valasaravakkam have reported a relatively higher number of dengue cases, according to the surveillance data. Health teams have consequently stepped up house-to-house visits, fever surveillance and source-reduction activities to identify and eliminate mosquito-breeding sites. Dengue, fever cases on the rise in Chennai; Adyar, Anna Nagar, Valasaravakkam turn hotspots The Greater Chennai Corporation has deployed about 3,700 mosquito-control workers across its 15 zones. Field teams have been instructed to inspect residential areas and other potential breeding sites, including vacant plots, construction sites and public institutions. Private hospitals have also been asked to share daily information on fever cases to strengthen surveillance. Health authorities have stressed that the rise in fever cases should not be equated with a dengue outbreak, as several other viral infections are also circulating in the city. Doctors have reported cases of influenza A, rhinovirus and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), among other respiratory infections. The Directorate of Public Health and Preventive Medicine has advised people with persistent fever to seek medical attention rather than self-medicate. Early consultation is particularly important when fever is accompanied by severe body pain, headache, vomiting, rash, bleeding or other warning symptoms. At the State level, dengue continues to remain a public-health concern. Health minister KG Arunraj told the Assembly last week that Tamil Nadu has recorded 14,581 dengue cases and nine deaths so far this year. With rainfall expected to increase in the coming weeks, DPH officials have urged residents to prevent water stagnation and keep water-storage containers covered. "Sustained mosquito-control measures, early detection and timely medical care will be crucial to contain infections," the officials said. Veloso Published on: Sep 15, 2026, 11:46 am Copied Summary The Provincial Health Office is not considering a dengue outbreak declaration in Cebu Province despite recording 3,759 cases and 21 deaths as of September 2026. Provincial health officer Dr. Sheila Faciol stated that dengue cases remain controlled, adding that hospitals are prepared with fast lanes, consultations, diagnostic kits, and round-the-clock laboratory services. The Provincial Government and the World Health Organization advised residents to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, keep surroundings clean, use protection, and watch for severe dengue warning signs. ADVERTISEMENT THE Provincial Health Office (PHO) is not considering declaring a dengue outbreak in Cebu Province despite thousands of reported infections and 21 deaths. Cebu Province recorded 3,759 dengue cases as of September 2026. Dr. Sheila Faciol, provincial health officer, said hospitals in the province are prepared to handle patients if dengue cases continue to rise, telling reporters on Monday, Sept. 14, that “dengue cases are still controlled.” Hospital preparations include dengue fast lanes and consultations for patients experiencing symptoms. The Provincial Government urged residents to keep their surroundings clean and empty containers holding stagnant water to eliminate breeding sites for mosquitoes that carry the dengue virus. ADVERTISEMENT Faciol said the province’s case numbers had not reached the threshold for a provincewide outbreak. PHO also reported that provincial and district hospitals have round-the-clock laboratory services, dengue diagnostic kits and sufficient intravenous fluids for incoming patients. ADVERTISEMENT WHO advice The World Health Organization advises households to cover water storage containers and empty and clean them weekly, while disposing of objects that can collect water. Mosquitoes that spread dengue are active during the day. Repellents, protective clothing and window screens help prevent bites. Warning signs of severe dengue include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing and bleeding from the gums or nose, and these can appear after the fever subsides. supplementary_news.content: Florida News Hillsborough Reports 95 Locally Acquired Dengue Cases By Rob GarguiloSep 11, 2026 Photo: martinatobolova / iStock / Getty Images Hillsborough, FL - Florida health officials are monitoring a sharp increase in locally acquired dengue fever cases, with Hillsborough County accounting for most infections statewide. The Florida Department of Health reported 111 locally acquired dengue cases across six counties through September 5th. Hillsborough County recorded 95 cases, representing about 86 percent of the statewide total. Miami-Dade County reported seven cases, Pinellas County had five, Pasco County had two, and Orange and Palm Beach counties each recorded one. Locally acquired infections involve people exposed to dengue within Florida rather than during international travel. State officials added 38 local cases during the reporting week covering August 30th through September 5th. The cases developed during July and August, including 13 Hillsborough infections in July and 82 in August. Laboratory testing identified the DENV-2 strain in 90 Hillsborough cases, while five were not assigned a specific strain. Dengue was also detected in 16 mosquito pools collected in Hillsborough County. Two positive pools involving Aedes aegypti mosquitoes were reported during the latest surveillance week. Florida separately recorded 160 travel-associated dengue cases during 2026, including eight in Hillsborough County. Dengue spreads primarily through bites from infected Aedes mosquitoes. Symptoms may include fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle or joint pain, nausea, vomiting and rash. Severe dengue can cause internal bleeding, shock or death and requires immediate medical treatment. Health officials advise residents to use insect repellent, wear protective clothing, maintain window screens and remove standing water where mosquitoes can reproduce. Hillsborough, Miami-Dade and Pinellas counties remained under mosquito-borne illness alerts. View Full Site

Add Axios on Google Illustration: Maura Losch/Axios Nearly 100 locally acquired dengue cases have been reported in Hillsborough County, and the state Department of Health is investigating a death possibly linked to the virus. Why it matters: The county is the epicenter of Florida's dengue outbreak, accounting for about 86% of locally acquired cases statewide. Driving the news: The family of a South Tampa woman who died this month told the Tampa Bay Times that she had dengue. The state is investigating whether the virus contributed to her death. Hillsborough County has recorded 95 locally acquired dengue cases since July, according to the state Department of Health. The county expanded aerial and ground mosquito treatments this week, including aerial treatments in Seminole Heights, Ybor City, West Tampa and Palma Ceia. Threat level: About 1 in 4 people infected with the virus will get sick, with symptoms ranging from mild to severe, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Fever is the most common symptom, often accompanied by headache, rash, vomiting and joint pain. In severe cases, dengue can be life-threatening within a few hours. Zoom out: Five cases have been reported in Pinellas County, and Pasco County has recorded two. But as Alissa Berro, director of Pinellas County Mosquito Control, put it, "dengue doesn't stop at county lines." People travel throughout the region every day. Be smart: Use insect repellent before going outdoors and wear long-sleeved shirts and closed-toe shoes. Light colors may help, too. Research suggests dark clothing makes people more visible to mosquitoes. Dump or cover standing water around your home. NewsPricingLoginSign up free News·Development Development WHO review highlights SynAct’s resomelagon among six dengue drugs for further development Edited by Robert McTiernan·September 16, 2026·2 min read A World Health Organization review of the dengue therapeutic pipeline has identified resomelagon as one of six candidates with sufficient supporting efficacy data to warrant further clinical development. The molecule's developer is Sweden-based SynAct Pharma AB (Nasdaq Stockholm: SYNACT). The review, published in Lancet Microbe, is intended to guide regulators, funders, and developers toward accelerated product development in a disease that WHO reported affected more than 14 million people in 2024. The WHO framework distinguishes treatments for non-severe dengue, where reducing symptom duration and preventing progression are key goals, from therapies for severe disease, where reducing organ failure and mortality is the priority. Resomelagon is the only host-directed therapy among the six named candidates, with the five others being small-molecule antivirals and monoclonal antibody antiviral programs. SynAct argues that this could allow treatment later in the disease course than direct antivirals, which are generally expected to work best early in infection. Resomelagon selectively activates the MC1 and MC3 melanocortin receptors to promote resolution of active inflammation rather than broadly suppressing immune activity. The ongoing Phase II RESOVIR-2 study — a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Brazil under the leadership of Professor Mauro Teixeira at the Federal University of Minas Gerais — is evaluating resomelagon in dengue patients with reduction in symptom duration as the primary endpoint. No efficacy or safety data have been reported; results from Part 1 are expected in 2026 pending feedback from regulatory authorities. The WHO review separately identified symptom resolution as an appropriate and clinically meaningful endpoint for non-severe dengue, an alignment SynAct said supports its development approach. The AllSci BriefFree, systematic R&D and deal news. Daily. Subscribe The WHO review also establishes target product profiles for dengue therapeutics that emphasize oral administration, a broad safety profile, and prevention of progression to severe disease — characteristics SynAct said are consistent with resomelagon's profile. A post-hoc analysis of the Phase IIb ADVANCE study, published in September 2026, reported that among patients with stable baseline high-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels, ACR20 response rates were 79% with resomelagon 40 mg versus 55% with placebo (p < 0.05), and SynAct has said it plans to discuss a Phase III trial design with the FDA in Q4 2026. SynAct has a collaboration with Brazilian company Hipolabor for development and commercialization of resomelagon in dengue, which it described as a first step toward broader strategic partnerships. supplementary_news.content: Wednesday 16 Sep 2026 Home Corporate Economy Court & Politics Sections EdgeTV Tech Opinion 新闻 Home Corporate Economy Court & Politics Sections EdgeTV Tech Opinion 新闻 Home Corporate Economy Court & Politics Sections EdgeTV Tech Opinion 新闻 BURSASGX Home Opinion: The 2026 El Niño phenomenon and its impact on dengue outbreaks Malaysia Opinion Politics & Government Opinion Opinion: The 2026 El Niño phenomenon and its impact on dengue outbreaks By Dr Musa Mohd Nordin & Dr Husna Musa 12 Sep 2026, 11:30 am Make The Edge Malaysia your preferred source on Google A pest control worker spraying insecticide to help control the spread of dengue fever carried by mosquitoes. The Aedes mosquito, which carries the dengue virus, is extremely sensitive to temperature. Warmer conditions are a boon to the mosquito. They help it live longer, bite more frequently, and, crucially, allow the dengue virus inside the mosquito to replicate faster. (Sept 12): Some of the most important warnings in public health don’t come from a doctor or a lab report. They come from the ocean. Right now, the Pacific Ocean is sending us one. The tropical Pacific has already entered El Niño conditions and the phenomenon is continuing to strengthen. Current forecasts indicate a greater than 90% probability that El Niño will persist through the Northern Hemisphere of winter 2026-2027, with a substantial likelihood of developing into a very strong event. For those of us who track dengue fever, this isn't just a weather update. El Niño remains one of the most valuable multi-month climate signals available to public health, providing an early warning of a heightened risk of dengue outbreaks across much of the tropical world. The signal is clear, and we have time to act. What is El Niño, and why does it matter for mosquitoes? Think of El Niño as the ocean breathing a warm breath. Normally, trade winds push warm surface water towards Asia and allow cold, nutrient-rich water to rise off the coast of South America. During El Niño, those winds weaken. The warm water slides back eastward across the Pacific, heating the ocean surface and, in turn, the atmosphere. This shift has ripple effects on weather patterns thousands of kilometres away. It often brings hotter, drier conditions to Southeast Asia and Australia, and wetter conditions to parts of South America and East Africa. These are the same regions that carry the heaviest burden of dengue. So, how does a warmer ocean lead to more dengue? The link is one of the most well-studied connections between climate and infectious disease, and it works through two main pathways. First, there is the biological effect. The Aedes mosquito, which carries the dengue virus, is extremely sensitive to temperature. Warmer conditions are a boon to the mosquito. They help it live longer, bite more frequently, and, crucially, allow the dengue virus inside the mosquito to replicate faster. This means a mosquito can become infectious and start spreading the virus sooner. A study in Brazil, for example, found that during El Niño years, the number of Aedes mosquito larvae jumped by 30% compared to normal years. Second, there is the hydrological and behavioural effect. El Niño doesn't just bring heat; it redistributes rainfall. Where it causes drought, families store more water in containers around the home — perfect breeding grounds for mosquitoes. Where it causes flooding, it creates countless new pools of stagnant water. Either way, the mosquito wins. This is not a new phenomenon. Studies from Venezuela and Brazil have shown that dengue outbreaks tend to follow a cyclical pattern, often every three to four years, that aligns with El Niño. What is troubling is that these cycles appear to be getting shorter, compressing to every two-to-three years. This suggests that more frequent El Niños and rising global temperatures are disrupting the virus's natural rhythm and making outbreaks more common. The data is undeniable If the mechanisms are clear, so is the data. A major study published last year in Nature Communications, which analysed 57 countries over four decades, provided a staggering quantification of the risk. It found that El Niño-related temperature changes could explain about 63% of the year-to-year variation in dengue cases. For every 1°C rise in a key Pacific Ocean temperature index, dengue cases increased by 48%. The study also showed that the scale of these outbreaks is growing exponentially. The four largest El Niño events on record produced an estimated excess of 0.2 million, 1.4 million, 4.1 million, and a staggering 9.6 million dengue cases, respectively. Each event is bigger than the last. Country-level data confirms this. A 2026 study on Indonesia found that during strong El Niño years, dengue incidence was 96% higher than in neutral years. The country's massive 2024 outbreak of roughly 250,000 cases fits squarely within this pattern. The 2014-2016 El Niño was one of the strongest El Niño events on record. It aligns very well with the surge of dengue cases and deaths in the 2014-2016 outbreaks in Malaysia (see Graphs I -III). Perhaps most importantly, a recent analysis in The Lancet Planetary Health delivered a sobering conclusion: about half of the increased dengue risk we see during El Niño is no longer just natural weather variability. It is being supercharged by human-caused climate change. Why 2026 is different The El Niño forecast for 2026 is a warning we cannot afford to ignore, for three reasons. The baseline is hotter. The world is warmer now than during previous El Niño events. The tropics, once too cool in some areas for the Aedes mosquito, are now becoming more hospitable to it. The events are stronger. Climate models project that El Niño events themselves will become more intense, with one study estimating a 39-82% increase in the dengue burden they drive by the end of the century. The danger lasts. The impact of an El Niño event is not a single season. Its climate signature can persist for up to two years, meaning a 2026 event is also a 2027 problem. From warning to action This forecast gives us something incredibly rare in public health: a head start. We know what’s coming, roughly when, and where. This means we can no longer afford a fragmented, reactive approach. The climate signal is already visible; we must act on it. This is the time to: Strengthen surveillance: Health ministries must use this climate data to prepare. Early-warning systems based on El Niño forecasts are not a luxury — they are a necessity. We need to ensure our systems for tracking cases are robust and ready. Pre-position resources: Vector control operations, hospital surge capacity, and essential supplies must be planned and ready to go before cases begin to rise, not after hospitals are overwhelmed. Empower communities: For clinicians and communicators, the message is one of foreseeable risk. We must engage communities now on how to eliminate mosquito breeding sites, protect themselves from bites, and consider vaccination where available. Integrate our response: We must see vector control, community engagement, climate-informed early warning, and vaccination not as separate tools, but as a single, integrated portfolio of defence. No single measure is enough. The science is converging across dozens of studies in very different settings. The conclusion is unanimous: El Niño is a probabilistic, multi-month early warning for dengue. And the signal is strengthening. The 2026 El Niño has arrived and the climatic signals are intensifying. Yet the value of El Niño lies precisely in the advance warning it provides. The forecast is here. The evidence is here. The lead time is here. The ocean has breathed its warm breath. The question is whether we will listen. What we do in the coming months and year ahead will determine whether the next outbreak arrives as a surprise or as a signal we had the opportunity to anticipate and prepare for. Dr Musa Mohd Nordin is a consultant paediatrician at Damansara Specialist Hospital. Dr Husna Musa is a consultant paediatric neurologist at Universiti Putra Malaysia. supplementary_news.content: Philstar Home The Philippine Star Pilipino Star Ngayon The Freeman CEBU NEWS OPINION METRO CEBU REGION CEBU BUSINESS CEBU SPORTS CEBU LIFESTYLE CEBU ENTERTAINMENT SUPPORT PHILSTAR Pang-Masa Banat Close the sidebar In Cebu City: Dengue toll triples By Caecent No-ot Magsumbol(The Freeman) - September 15, 2026 - 12:00am Facebook Twitter The City Health Department reported 2,456 cases from January to September 5, up sharply from 1,485 cases recorded during the same period in 2025. CEBU, Philippines — Dengue-related deaths in Cebu City have climbed to 20, more than tripling the six fatalities recorded during the same period last year. The City Health Department reported 2,456 cases from January to September 5, up sharply from 1,485 cases recorded during the same period in 2025. Kenneth Siasar, chief of staff of Mayor Nestor Archival, admitted the gravity of the situation during a press briefing at City Hall yesterday. “Since January until now, we have 2,456 cases. In comparison sa last year, the same month, January to September, we have 1,484. So karon taas-taas, 2,456. Ug na, ang atong mortality, kani atong death, um, since January until now, we have 20 deaths as reported sa City Health Department. Compared to last year, January to September, six ra ang atong death nga cases,” Siasar said. Hospital data from the Cebu City Medical Center (CCMC) showed 844 dengue cases between January 1 and September 13, including 297 admissions and 547 consultations. CCMC recorded 16 deaths, while the City Health Department’s higher tally of 20 includes cases reported by private hospitals. Siasar attributed the rise in cases and deaths partly to lapses in household sanitation. “We are unable to sustain ang pagpanglimpyo sa atong palibot. Ang source sa lamok sa dengue na-a sa gawas, but na-a pod kini sa sulod... flower vases, drums, PVC pipes with stagnated water puy-an pod na siya’g nguyonguyo,” he said. Children remain particularly vulnerable, with several fatalities involving young patients. “Ang vulnerable jud kanang dili kayo makaprotect sa ilang kaugalingon, especially mga bata nga bisan asa lang magduwa,” Siasar noted, adding that elderly residents and office workers have also been affected. The city government has intensified misting operations, including inside City Hall after an employee contracted dengue. Siasar said Archival instructed health teams not to wait for requests from barangays but to act based on surveillance data. “Kung mahimo, we are not to wait for the request coming from the different barangays, but we have to look into asa ni mga barangaya ang mas taas ang kaso sa dengue and then atong i-intensify,” he said. The barangays with the highest dengue caseloads include Guadalupe, Lahug, Basak San Nicolas, Tisa, Labangon, Talamban, Mambaling, Kalunasan, and Punta Princesa, as well as Apas, which is tied with Sambag II and Tejero. Prevention The Department of Health and the World Health Organization identify dengue as a viral infection transmitted through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, swollen glands and rash. Severe dengue can cause abdominal pain, persistent vomiting and bleeding and may be fatal. The DOH promotes the “4S” strategy: Search and destroy breeding sites, Self-protection, Seek early consultation, and Support fogging or misting when necessary. In Central Visayas, the “4Ts” campaign — Taob, Taktak, Tuyo, Takip — is also being emphasized to eliminate stagnant water and keep water containers covered. Archival announced late last week that Cebu City is moving forward with the World Mosquito Program’s Wolbachia Method as a complementary dengue-prevention strategy. “We are moving forward with the implementation of the World Mosquito Program’s (WMP) Wolbachia Method as a complementary dengue-prevention strategy in Cebu City. Pinaagi sa Office and team ni Dr. Michelle Abella-Cellona, atong gipalig-on ang coordination and preparation for the program, kauban ang Cebu City Health Department (CHD), World Mosquito Program, ug ang atong Liga ng mga Barangay (ABC),” Mayor Archival said. Through a newly organized Technical Working Group (TWG) under Executive Order No. 109, Series of 2026, the city government is aligning the plans, technical requirements, community engagement and coordination needed for the program’s implementation. “Importante nga maampingon ug well-coordinated ang matag step as we work toward preventing dengue and other mosquito-borne diseases and protecting the health of our communities. Padayon ta sa pagtinabangay para sa mas healthy ug mas safe nga Cebu City,” Archival added. — (FREEMAN) SPONSORED ARTICLES Full circle moment: SM scholar-graduate building their future with SM group Supplements September 16, 2026 - 3:57pm SM Supermalls President Steven Tan named among honorees at The Business Manual’s CEO Awards Lifestyle Business September 16, 2026 - 3:15pm Order fiber WiFi like food delivery: GFiber Prepaid expands WiFi-on-demand via GrabMart to Metro Manila, Cebu, Davao Technology September 16, 2026 - 1:57pm Monde Nissin unveils better food forward, bringing stakeholders together to advance accessible nutrition Food and Leisure September 16, 2026 - 10:00am Culture and creativity take over in SM Malls Cagayan de Oro On the Radar September 15, 2026 - 4:22pm Mindanao’s story, woven into every look Fashion and Beauty September 15, 2026 - 3:57pm After 64 years, Metrobank keeps evolving and growing stronger with Filipinos Banking September 15, 2026 - 3:42pm Beauty + Health & Wellness Manila marks 10th year with bigger lineup of brands and activities Fashion and Beauty September 15, 2026 - 1:30pm Home Credit PH renews partnership with UST Tigers and Tigresses for UAAP Season Sports September 15, 2026 - 12:00pm Show comments Ad

supplementary_news.content_title: Aerial operations to curb dengue fever begin in Hillsborough County
supplementary_news.content: Aerial operations to curb dengue fever begin in Hillsborough County - A low-flying helicopter in Hillsborough County is part of ongoing mosquito treatment efforts to prevent the spread of dengue fever. If you live in Hillsborough County, you may have noticed a low-flying helicopter around your neighborhood during the day this week. The chopper is part of ongoing mosquito treatment efforts to stop the spread of dengue fever across the county. This week's efforts are targeting mosquito larvae — juvenile mosquitoes that can live in water for up to two weeks before becoming adults. Beginning at 9:30 a.m. Wednesday, the helicopter will apply liquid Bti (Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis) across central Tampa, including locations south of Busch Boulevard, north of San Miguel Street, west of North 50th Street and east of Manhattan Avenue Bti is a naturally occurring larvicide that is safe for humans, pets, fish and birds and breaks down naturally in the environment. If you live or work in the areas mentioned above, you may see an orange and black helicopter flying at a low altitude during the day. The helicopter might make repeated passes over certain areas, and you may see visible application of the liquid larvicide. Residents should expect significant noise from the helicopter as it will fly just above structures. The treatment, which is being done with assistance from the Pasco County Mosquito Control District, is expected to take two days. The helicopter will go up again Thursday morning, weather permitting. Crews are increasing treatments as mosquito traps in many neighborhoods are showing dengue fever virus activity. Hillsborough County's Mosquito Management team has worked closely with the Florida Department of Health for surveillance, education and treatment in the impacted area. Residents can do their part to control the mosquito population by following the three Ds: - Dress in light-colored, long-sleeved clothing with closed-toed shoes - Defend using an insect repellent with a CDC-recommended ingredient such as DEET, Picaridin, IR3535, or oil of lemon eucalyptus - Dump or cover standing water

supplementary_news.content: Dawn E-Paper | September 17, 2026 Home Latest Violations Tracker Pakistan Opinion Business Images Prism World Sport Breathe Magazines Tech Videos Popular Archive Flood Donations Dengue tally reaches seven in Rawalpindi The Newspaper's Staff Reporter Published September 16, 2026 Updated September 16, 2026 09:19am comments Join our Whatsapp Channel Add Dawn as a trusted source RAWALPINDI: A dengue patient was reported in the garrison city on Tuesday, taking the total tally to seven in the current season. A patient from Dhama Syedan was brought to Holy Family Hospital, where he was shifted to the dengue ward. Earlier, a patient from Asghar Mall Scheme was reported on Sept 9. District Health Officer Preventive Dr Jawad Zahid told Dawn that two dengue patients had been reported in September, four detected in July and one in March. However, he said the spread of the dengue virus was under control, as 582 patients were reported in the garrison city last year, compared to only seven this year. He said an anti-dengue campaign had been launched in the garrison city and 1,400 teams had been formed for indoor and outdoor surveillance. He said the highest number of larvae had been detected in Misrial Road, Afshan Colony and Allama Iqbal Colony in Rawalpindi Cantonment, while significant larvae detection areas included Naseerabad, Morgah, Dhama Syedan, Pirwadhai, Dhamyal, Hazara Colony, Pindora, Dhoke Mangtal, Dhoke Ratta and Chak Jalaldin. During the anti-dengue campaign in the current season, larvae were found at more than 145,572 locations in houses and open spaces, all of which were destroyed. He said action had been taken over violations of dengue SOPs, with 2,543 FIRs registered, 652 buildings sealed and 2,119 challans issued. Fines amounting to Rs2.568 million were imposed on violators. He said the number of field staff had been increased as part of the anti-dengue campaign. The more larvae that were located and destroyed, he said, the more the dengue threat could be reduced. He urged citizens to keep their houses and rooftops clean and prevent stagnant water from accumulating to stop dengue breeding in their homes under any circumstances. supplementary_news.content_title: 每个家庭都需要采取积极措施来阻止登革热病例的增加。
supplementary_news.content: Tiếng Việt 首页 话题 时事 政治制度 当地的 事件 旅游 快乐越南 企业 产品 遗产 博物馆 数字 多媒体 数据 Văn hóa - Xã hội 医疗的 每个家庭都需要采取积极措施来阻止登革热病例的增加。 登革热疫情已进入高峰期,河内的病例数量呈上升趋势。 Báo Đầu tư•28/12/2025 Google Google 0 雨季和高湿度为携带疾病的蚊子提供了适宜的繁殖条件,导致河内登革热病例再次激增。许多地方政府不等疫情爆发,就积极主动地实施了全面的防控措施,将民众置于疾病防控工作的核心位置。 据统计,今年以来, 河内市福禄乡共报告了4例登革热病例。虽然病例数量不多,但当地政府积极主动地采取了疾病预防措施,而不是坐等疫情爆发。 目前,Qdenga是越南首个获得许可使用的登革热疫苗。 该公社加强了疾病预防控制指导委员会;成立了387个蚊幼虫灭杀工作组和92个监测小组,并在高风险地区组织了多次环境卫生运动,以提高人们的意识,并动员人们参与疾病预防。 福禄乡人民委员会常务副主席丁春行表示,疾病预防控制和公共卫生保健一直是当地政府重点工作。 “乡人民委员会积极制定了2026-2030年登革热防控计划,指示相关部门、组织和村庄协调实施基层综合防控措施。 卫生部门积极开展监测、早期发现和及时处理工作,以防止疫情扩散。”汉先生说。 Khám phá thêm Dịch Từ Điển Ghé Điểm Đến du lịch 据他介绍,当地定期开展环境卫生活动,检查并处理蚊子幼虫滋生地;准备充足的物资、化学品和设备用于疾病预防;并不断加强快速反应部队,培训沟通和监测技能,以促进社区在疾病早期控制中发挥作用。 在基层,福禄乡卫生站正在加强疫情监测、早期发现和及时彻底处理。据福禄乡卫生站副主任段仲基先生介绍,该站已制定2026年登革热防控计划,并与各组织协调开展多项环境卫生运动,审查风险区域,彻底清除蚊虫滋生地。 Ky先生说:“一旦发现病例,卫生站会与应急响应小组协调,调查和监测风险因素,组织化学喷洒以杀死成蚊,并加强公众宣传活动,鼓励人们积极采取预防措施。” 根据河内疾病控制中心(CDC)的统计数据,上周该市66个乡镇共记录了175例登革热病例,比前一周增加了29例。 从年初到2026年7月31日,河内市113个乡镇共报告1046例新冠肺炎确诊病例,无死亡病例报告。该市共发生42起疫情,其中17起仍在持续。 河内市疾控中心正与相关部门协调,加强疫情监测、控制和彻底处理。同时,要求各地定期开展环境卫生运动,清除蚊虫幼虫,在高风险地区喷洒化学药剂,并加大宣传力度,鼓励民众积极预防疾病。 据河内市疾病预防控制中心副主任陶友坦博士称,登革热预防和控制的有效性很大程度上取决于每个家庭的意识,因为大多数蚊子滋生地就存在于居民区内。 每个家庭每周至少应抽出10分钟时间检查并清除水容器中的蚊虫滋生地;盖紧水箱盖,定期更换花瓶中的水,在鱼缸中养鱼,并将不用的物品翻过来放置,以防止蚊虫滋生。陶友丹医生建议:“同时,人们应积极接种疫苗,并积极配合卫生部门开展蚊虫幼虫灭杀活动和疾病预防的化学喷洒工作。” 专家还指出,当出现突发高烧、头痛、身体疼痛、皮下出血等症状,或怀疑患有登革热时,应及时前往医疗机构进行检查和治疗,绝对不要在家自行治疗,以免出现危险的并发症。 为应对这一威胁,卫生部门正在实施一系列综合活动,包括流行病学监测、疫情管理以及加强公众宣传活动,以提高社区对疾病预防和控制的认识。 据龙洲药房和疫苗系统医疗委员会副主任黎清奎医生称,持续的暴雨使得水容器、人孔、遮阳篷、屋顶、阳台和其他清洁不彻底的地方成为伊蚊(登革热病毒的传播媒介)的理想滋生地。 除了气候因素外,快速的城市化、人口密度高以及大量的公寓楼和寄宿公寓也增加了疾病传播的风险。 世界卫生组织(世卫组织)指出,排水系统不完善和大量人工蓄水池的存在是登革热在人口密集的城市地区持续存在的原因。 值得注意的是,登革病毒有四种不同的血清型,这意味着一个人一生中可能会多次感染登革热。如果未能及时发现和治疗,再次感染会增加出现严重并发症的风险。虽然登革热以前被认为是一种儿童疾病,但现在成人病例已占所有病例的一半以上。 专家指出,许多成年人因疏忽或在家自行治疗,导致病情发展到晚期才入院。当出现持续高烧、头痛、肌肉酸痛、皮疹等症状,或出现剧烈腹痛、持续呕吐、异常出血等预警信号时,患者应立即前往医疗机构进行检查和监测,以避免出现危险的并发症。 据卫生部称,登革热是由登革病毒引起的传染病,通过埃及伊蚊传播给人类。全球约有56亿人生活在登革热风险地区;每年记录在案的登革病毒感染病例在1亿至4亿例之间。该疾病主要流行于热带和亚热带地区,但由于气候变化、城市化和人口流动加剧的影响,其传播范围正在扩大。 大多数登革热患者症状轻微或无症状。然而,部分病例若未能及时发现和治疗,可能发展为重症登革热,并出现休克、严重出血、器官衰竭甚至死亡等危险并发症。目前,尚无针对登革热的特效药。 2025年,越南累计报告新冠肺炎病例超过18.1万例,死亡43例。2026年头几个月,新增病例近6万例,几乎是上年同期的三倍。值得注意的是,疫情不再遵循以往的周期性波动,而是自年初以来就显著增加,甚至在通常病例激增的雨季到来之前就已如此。 据卫生部疾病预防司副司长武海山介绍,登革热疫情正逐渐打破以往的流行模式。往年登革热病例数通常在年底有所下降,但2025年11月和12月的病例数仍将居高不下。 年初以来,持续高温高湿、雨水不断的天气为携带疾病的蚊子繁殖和发育创造了有利条件。此外,登革病毒2型(DENV-2)的流行也导致了重症病例和住院人数的增加。 许多地区目前正进入蚊虫繁殖高峰期。冷热交替的天气、高湿度以及家庭和居民区内大量盛水容器的存在,都为伊蚊的繁殖创造了有利条件。 专家强调,目前登革热的治疗主要包括密切监测、补液和并发症处理,因为尚无特效药可以根除登革病毒。因此,积极预防被认为是降低感染风险和减轻疾病严重程度的最重要“屏障”。 除了清除蚊子幼虫、清除死水、睡在蚊帐下、防止蚊虫叮咬等传统措施外,接种疫苗也被认为是预防登革热的有效主动解决方案。 目前,Qdenga是越南首个获准使用的登革热疫苗。该疫苗含有减毒活登革病毒,能够刺激人体产生针对所有四种登革病毒(DEN-1、DEN-2、DEN-3和DEN-4)的免疫反应。 许多国家的研究数据和实际应用表明,完成两剂接种后,该疫苗在 12 个月后对预防登革热的有效率超过 80%,并在 18 个月后有助于将住院风险降低 90% 以上。 专家认为这是抗击登革热的重要一步,尤其是在登革热病情日益复杂且在许多城市地区呈上升趋势的情况下。 随着疫情进入高峰期,许多疫苗接种系统已推出疫苗,以提高公众接种的便利性。 据龙洲疫苗接种系统一位代表介绍,Qdenga登革热疫苗目前已在越南上市。该疫苗适用于4岁及以上儿童和成人,包括曾患过登革热的人群,有助于预防所有四种类型的登革热病毒感染。 疫苗接种程序包括两剂,间隔三个月。保护效力超过80%,完成全部接种程序后,可将因登革热住院的风险降低90%以上。 专家认为,疫苗的最大意义不仅在于降低患病风险,还在于限制重症病例,减轻疫情期间医疗系统的负担,并有助于保护儿童等高危人群。 然而,对疫苗任何成分过敏者、孕妇或哺乳期妇女不宜接种。免疫功能低下者或艾滋病毒感染者,请咨询医疗专业人员,以获得针对您具体情况的指导。 supplementary_news.content: Tiếng Việt 首页 话题 时事 政治制度 当地的 事件 旅游 快乐越南 企业 产品 遗产 博物馆 数字 多媒体 数据 Văn hóa - Xã hội 医疗的 登革热:危险始于三个常见的误解。 登革热可导致登革出血性休克、多器官衰竭(如肝衰竭、肾衰竭、心肌炎、脑损伤等)。 Báo Sức khỏe và Đời sống•11/09/2026 Google Google 0 达乐和嘉莱 登革热造成的首例死亡病例刚刚记录在案——一名年轻男子和一名老年人,两人均有 2 型糖尿病史。 这表明该疾病在任何年龄都可能发展得很严重,有基础疾病的人尤其需要警惕。 登革热正在全国蔓延。 今年前八个月,全国共记录了超过78338例登革热病例。 (登革热),包括 13 例死亡——病例数是 2025 年同期的 1.2 倍。南部地区仍然是登革热的热点地区,其中胡志明市病例数最多(31,032 例); 同奈省11,519 例,包括 6 例死亡;西宁省 8,437 例,包括 1 例死亡。 在北部, 河内市超过 92% 的街道/乡(126 个街道/乡中有 117 个)记录了登革热病例,总共有 2382 例。 登革热不仅病例数量不断增加,而且病情发展迅速且难以预测,尤其是在患有糖尿病、肝病或慢性肾病等基础疾病的人群中。然而,许多人仍然低估了这种疾病的严重性。 统计数据背后是需要急诊和重症监护治疗的患者,以及病情迅速恶化的患者。专家指出,许多病例因疏忽或社会上仍然存在的对这种疾病的误解而延误就医。 这些故事在播客节目“登革热:图片背后的惊人真相”中得以重述,该节目由胡志明市热带病医院传染病科主任潘荣寿医生和摄影师吴陈海安主持。节目有助于人们更清晰地了解一些常见的误解,这些误解可能会使患者面临严重并发症的风险。 Khám phá thêm du lịch DU LỊCH Đặt Vé Event 摄影师 Ngo Tran Hai An 和专家医生 Phan Vinh Tho 通过拍摄医院的照片,深入探究了登革热背后的危险。 误区一:登革热只是发烧和出血。 据Tho医生介绍,严重出血是许多人最担心的并发症。然而,出血不仅仅指呕血或体表出血;它还可能包括内出血、腹腔出血或其他难以发现的部位出血。 更危险的是,登革出血热可导致登革休克和多器官衰竭,如肝衰竭、肾衰竭、心肌炎、脑损伤......如果不及时发现和治疗,会危及生命。 对于老年人来说,肝损伤是一种特别令人担忧的并发症。 “登革热引起的肝损伤是一个持续存在的威胁。有些病例会出现严重的炎症、肝酶水平极高以及严重的肝细胞坏死, ” Tho 医生说。 摄影师海安在医院目睹的景象也让他对登革热的严重程度感到惊讶: “我甚至问医生这真的是登革热引起的吗?为什么登革热这么可怕?” 误区二:退烧就意味着危险已经过去。 许多人认为退烧就意味着即将康复。但对于登革热来说,退烧反而可能是最危险的时期。 据Tho医生介绍,危重期通常发生在第3天到第7天之间,此时患者的体温开始下降。患者可能出现血浆渗漏、低血压、休克和其他严重并发症。值得注意的是,即使病情发展到重症阶段,患者可能仍然意识清醒,能够正常行走。2022年,Tho医生遇到一名男学生,他出现了一些预警症状,但由于感觉良好而拒绝住院。第二天早上,这名学生出现紫绀,病情危重,被送回医院。 如果您出现以下警告信号,例如发烧消退但疲劳加剧、剧烈腹痛、频繁呕吐、流鼻血、牙龈出血、呕血、手脚冰凉等。 患者应立即前往最近的医疗机构就诊,无需等待预约时间。 误区三:登革热只是儿童疾病。 许多人仍然认为登革热是一种儿童疾病。但事实上,近年来成人病例数量已显著增加。 60 岁以上的人、孕妇以及患有肥胖症、心血管疾病、高血压、肝脏或肾脏疾病等基础疾病的人更容易出现严重症状,可能需要住院密切监测。 此外,登革热最多可感染四次。即使之前感染过,也不意味着完全免疫,而且由于登革病毒特有的免疫机制,第二次感染甚至可能出现更严重的并发症。 这些误解不仅会加重患者的病情,还会给家庭和医疗系统带来沉重的负担。海安在医院进行摄影报道项目期间,捕捉到了许多反映登革热破坏性影响的瞬间:幼小的孩子们在错综复杂的输液管中接受治疗,连续几个不眠之夜后精疲力竭的家属,以及忙碌地监测病情进展的医生和护士。 “拍摄结束后,我回到了家,但那种感觉在我心中萦绕了一两天,”他说道。 “一个孩子或一个健康的人可能只会发烧3-4天,然后病情可能会急剧恶化,需要机械通气和透析。如果他们不幸去世,对家庭来说将是巨大的损失,”Tho医生说道。 每一场重病背后,不仅有重症监护室里的一场战斗,还有数亿越南盾的治疗费用、耽误上学和工作的日子、收入损失,以及无数不得不搁置的计划。 主动预防疾病要从最小的事情做起。 鉴于登革热全年都会发生,而且没有特效药,积极预防仍然是最重要的。 人们应主动避免蚊虫叮咬,如果怀疑自己患有登革热,应立即就医。检查和适当的检测有助于及早发现疾病,从而进行及时的监测和治疗。 Tho 医生表示,将接种疫苗与登革热预防措施相结合,有助于降低高危人群出现严重并发症的风险。 Tho医生强调,目前除了传统的预防措施外,接种疫苗是一种辅助手段,有助于主动预防登革热,降低感染风险及其严重程度。他表示,如果将疫苗接种与幼虫控制、蚊虫灭杀以及早期发现并及时治疗相结合,每个人都可以主动保护自己和家人免受登革热的侵害。 *** 本节目由武田药品工业株式会社与越南政府电子报合作推出,并经越南预防医学协会专业咨询和批准。所有医学信息均客观呈现,不代表任何公司的商业观点。 supplementary_news.content: Tiếng Việt 首页 话题 时事 政治制度 当地的 事件 旅游 快乐越南 企业 产品 遗产 博物馆 数字 多媒体 数据 Văn hóa - Xã hội 医疗的 不要低估登革热。 虽然现在才刚刚进入夏季,但登革热病例却呈上升趋势,目前已报告31927例病例和4例死亡。在接下来的这段时间里,登革热病例可能会继续增加,尤其是在雨季期间。 Báo Đầu tư•28/12/2025 Google Google 0 据卫生部消息,今年年初就已出现登革热病例,主要集中在南部各省市。在河内,自2026年初至今,已有75个乡镇报告了200多例病例。 近年来,越南的登革热疫情持续呈现周期性上升趋势,高发年份与低发年份交替出现。 19-8 医院从年初开始,热带病科就接诊了登革热病例,尽管当时还不是流行季节的高峰期,而且该疾病的发展往往复杂且难以预测。 一个典型的例子是来自河内玉河的 67 岁男性患者 PBD,他有糖尿病、高血压病史,得过一次登革热,但没有接种过疫苗。 入院前两天,D 先生突然出现 39-40 摄氏度的高烧、烦躁不安、嗜睡、剧烈头痛(偶尔伴有痉挛)、肌肉疼痛以及双眼眶疼痛。 Khám phá thêm Tìm Sự Kiện Tra Bản Đồ Đặt Vé Tàu 尤其是在患病的第 4 天和第 6 天,他出现了频繁呕吐(每天 5-6 次)、少尿、血小板计数在 48 小时内从 246 迅速下降到 11,然后下降到 6 G/l、多膜渗出、血液浓缩和呼吸困难。 根据治疗方案,患者接受了液体和电解质补充、氧气支持、血小板输注、止血、血细胞计数监测、基础疾病管理以及继发感染控制。 据19-8医院热带病科主任杜氏清翠女士介绍,早期发现疾病并彻底了解疾病各个阶段的临床问题有助于早期诊断、正确及时的治疗,最终挽救患者的生命。 众所周知,近年来越南的登革热疫情呈现周期性波动,高发年份与低发年份交替出现。然而,除了周期性因素外,目前还有许多其他因素促成了登革热的流行,例如气候变暖、降雨不稳定、城市化进程加快、人口密度高以及居民区内蓄水设施众多等。 如果社区不能持续采取预防措施,这些因素会导致疫情更早出现、持续时间更长、更难控制。因此,监测和预防工作需要持续进行,而不仅仅是在高峰期。 据卫生部疾病预防司副司长武海山先生称,鉴于一些地区提前出现炎热潮湿的天气,以及当地居民的生活条件和储水情况,为传播疾病的蚊子滋生创造了有利条件,登革热疫情在未来一段时间内可能会继续加剧,尤其是在雨季。 孙先生还表示,目前仍有一部分社会成员对登革热的预防和控制缺乏充分的了解。 有些人认为传播疾病的蚊子只会在脏水中繁殖,但实际上,伊蚊经常在房屋内外装有干净或相对干净的水的容器中产卵,例如罐子、花瓶、水桶、水盘和旧轮胎。 许多人仍然主要依赖化学喷洒,而最重要且可持续的措施仍然是清除蚊子滋生地并每周杀死蚊子幼虫。伊蚊通常在白天叮咬,因此人们不仅需要在夜间,也需要在白天积极做好防蚊措施。 据杜氏清翠博士称,预防登革热的有效措施包括为 4 岁及以上的儿童和成人接种登革热疫苗,该疫苗可预防 80% 以上的感染,并将住院风险降低 90% 以上,效果可持续 4-6 年。 然而,据专家称,尽管登革热疫苗已经问世,但接种率仍然很低,部分原因是疫苗价格相对较高,每剂超过 100 万越南盾(间隔 3 个月接种两剂)。 据龙洲疫苗接种系统一位代表介绍,Qdenga登革热疫苗目前在越南有售。该疫苗适用于4岁及以上儿童和成人,包括曾患过登革热的人群,有助于预防所有四种类型的登革热病毒感染。 疫苗接种程序包括两剂,间隔三个月。保护效力超过80%,完成全部接种程序后,可将因登革热住院的风险降低90%以上。 谈到登革热疫苗,登革热高级顾问武生南教授强调,越南只有从被动应对的心态转变为主动出击的策略,并结合多种预防措施,才能有效控制这种疾病。 世界卫生组织指出,积极主动的策略必须整合病媒控制、流行病学监测、行为改变沟通、循证治疗和疫苗接种预防。这些要素之间的持续协调将有助于降低疫情暴发的风险并减少重症病例。 登革热预防宣传不应只关注呼吁消灭蚊子和幼虫,还应着眼于可持续的行为改变,例如环境卫生、清除死水源,以及培养在日常生活中识别严重疾病预警信号的能力,使其成为一种自然反应。 预防措施始终是最重要的屏障。除了控制蚊子和幼虫外,登革热疫苗也带来了希望。武田制药的TAK-003(QDENGA)疫苗是一种重组减毒活四价疫苗,它利用DENV-2病毒框架表达所有四种登革病毒的结构蛋白,即使在从未感染过登革热的人群中也能产生平衡的免疫反应。 除了接种疫苗外,人们还需要积极主动地消灭蚊子、幼虫和蛹,清洁房屋,清理灌木丛,清除积水并成为蚊子滋生地的物体;睡在蚊帐下,并密切监测居住区的病例数量。 同时,必须及早发现症状,尤其是预警信号,前往信誉良好的医疗机构进行检查和治疗,避免自行输液或在家中使用来源不明的药物。这些都是保护您自身、家人和社区健康,抵御日益增长的登革热风险的切实可行的措施。
